questions.question: What does it mean for a real sequence $(a_n)_{n = 1}^{\infty}$ to be bounded?
options: There exists $M$ such that $|a_i|\ \le M$ for all $i\ \ge 1$
The sequence has only one term, under all circumstances whatsoever.
questions.explanation: A real sequence is bounded when one finite $M\ge0$ controls every term on both sides: $-M\le a_i\le M$, equivalently $|a_i|\le M$.

option_explanations: Equality $a_i=M$ would make the sequence constant, which is much stronger than boundedness.
Nonpositive terms can still be unbounded below, as $a_i=-i$ shows.

Having one term is a statement about the cardinality of the index set, whereas boundedness is a magnitude bound $\exists M:\ |a_i|\le M$ for every $i\ge 1$; sequences with infinitely many terms such as $a_i=1/i$ satisfy this since $|a_i|\le 1$.
